passage:
Dear Kiran,
You asked how the class picnic went. Honestly, the way I expected. I knew nobody really wanted me there; they only invited me because the whole class was going. So I sat at the edge of the mat with my earphones in and didn't say much. I didn't laugh at the jokes because I figured they weren't meant for me. Around noon, people stopped asking if I wanted to play. By the afternoon nobody even looked my way. See? I was right. Though one thing bothers me. When I got there, Tanya had waved and patted the space beside her. I pretended not to see. Maybe that was the moment. Maybe not. Anyway, how is your new school?
Pooja

qa.q: What did Pooja have in during the picnic?
qa.a: Earphones.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling while sitting at the edge of the mat?
qa.a: Pooja felt unwanted and lonely, convinced the others didn't like Pooja, and guarded against being rejected.

qa.q: What small step could Pooja try at the next gathering?
qa.a: Pooja could take up an invitation like Tanya's, sit with someone and join in once, then see how people actually respond.

qa.q: How might Tanya have seen Pooja ignoring her wave?
qa.a: Tanya might have felt snubbed and decided Pooja wasn't interested, so she stopped trying.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who expects classmates to dislike them, withdraws, and so draws the very distance that seems to confirm it.

passage: Varun, you asked why I didn't come to the tuition farewell. I'll tell you. The whole year I've been sure those guys think I'm boring. So at every group thing, I just stand there, scrolling, looking like I don't care. At the Diwali lunch, somebody asked if I wanted to join the cricket game. I shrugged. They didn't ask again. After that, nobody sat with me. And every time, I thought: told you. They don't like me. Then yesterday, you know what the teacher's son said? "We thought you didn't like us, man. You always look bored." Bored? I was terrified. So yeah. Maybe I did half of it myself. I, Ramesh, might go to the next thing and actually say something.

qa.q: What game did someone invite Ramesh to at the Diwali lunch?
qa.a: The cricket game.

qa.q: What was Ramesh actually feeling while scrolling at group events?
qa.a: Ramesh felt terrified and sure of being disliked, even though it looked like boredom to others.

qa.q: What could Ramesh do at the next event to test the belief?
qa.a: Ramesh could accept one invitation or start one short conversation, and treat how people respond as fresh evidence.

qa.q: How did the others see Ramesh's behaviour?
qa.a: They thought Ramesh didn't like them and looked bored, so they stopped asking.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose expectation of rejection makes the teen look bored and aloof, so others withdraw and seem to prove the belief right.

passage: Before: On his first Monday in the new school, Yogesh decided the class had already made up its mind about him. The new boy from the small town; they'd never want him. During: On Saturday, the class met for a cricket practice. Yogesh stood at the boundary, arms folded, face blank. When Kunal asked, "Want to bowl?" Yogesh said, "Whatever." Kunal gave the ball to someone else. By the end, nobody spoke to Yogesh. On the bus home, he thought, I knew it. After: Two weeks later, Kunal sat next to him in the library. "Can I ask something? Do you not like us? You always look so bored." Yogesh stared. "I thought you didn't like me." Kunal laughed. "We thought you were stuck up."

qa.q: What did Kunal ask Yogesh at cricket practice?
qa.a: "Want to bowl?"

qa.q: Why did Yogesh say "Whatever" to Kunal?
qa.a: He felt anxious and sure the class would reject him, so he hid behind a cold, bored look.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do now that he knows what Kunal thought?
qa.a: He could say yes next time, bowl, chat a little, and let the class see who he really is.

qa.q: How did Kunal and the others see Yogesh's folded arms and blank face?
qa.a: They read them as boredom and pride, thinking Yogesh was stuck up.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who expects rejection, acts aloof, and gets left alone, until he learns how his behaviour looked.

passage: At the ITI workshop in the kasba, Tarun, in his final year, was asked to guide two first-years. Minakshi asked a hundred questions on day one, so Tarun gave her the motor rewinding job, the hardest in the shop. He checked her work every day and explained each mistake. The other junior, a quiet boy, got sweeping and sorting screws, because he seemed slow. By the third month, Minakshi could rewind a motor alone. The quiet boy still sorted screws. One evening he stood by the rewinding bench, watching. Tarun realised he had never shown him anything. He had decided the boy was slow and then given him nothing to grow with. The next morning, Tarun handed him a small motor. "Let's start."

qa.q: What job did Tarun give Minakshi?
qa.a: The motor rewinding job, the hardest in the shop.

qa.q: What did Tarun feel when he realised he had never shown the quiet boy anything?
qa.a: Tarun felt uncomfortable and guilty, seeing that his own low expectation had kept the boy from growing.

qa.q: What small step did Tarun take to correct it?
qa.a: He handed the quiet boy a small motor and offered to start teaching him, giving him the challenge and attention Minakshi had had.

qa.q: What might it have been like for the quiet boy to sort screws for three months?
qa.a: He may have felt overlooked and discouraged, watching someone else learn while he stayed stuck.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing that a trusted junior rose to hard work while one given simple tasks stagnated, shaped by his expectations.

passage: Soo-ah, twenty-two, was a teaching assistant for a first-year coding class in Seoul. She'd decided early that Mei was the bright one: sharp questions, quick answers. So Mei got the tricky bonus problems and long comments on every assignment. A shy student in the back got a thumbs-up emoji and simpler tasks. By midterm, Mei was building her own small apps. The shy student's code looked exactly like it had in week one. Soo-ah was marking late one night when she noticed that her comments to the shy student were three words long, and Mei's were three paragraphs. She stopped typing. Maybe the difference wasn't only in them. The next week, she gave both of them the same bonus problem and the same amount of feedback.

qa.q: How old was Soo-ah?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling when she stopped typing?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little guilty, realising her own expectations gave Mei far more attention than the shy student.

qa.q: Which change did Soo-ah make, and why is it fairer?
qa.a: She gave both students the same bonus problem and the same amount of feedback, so both get a real chance to grow.

qa.q: How might the shy student have felt receiving only thumbs-up emojis?
qa.a: The shy student may have felt unnoticed and assumed there was nothing more to aim for.

grounding: Illustrates a mentor noticing that expectations shaped how much feedback and challenge two juniors received.

passage: Disha coordinated the college robotics lab in her final year, and two juniors joined in July. She liked the loud, confident one immediately and gave him the sensor project. Akash was quiet, so she asked him to label parts and keep the logbook. By October the confident junior was presenting at the tech fest. Akash was still labelling. Then one evening, Disha found Akash's logbook. In the margins he had drawn neat redesigns of the sensor mount, better than the one they were using. She sat down heavily. She hadn't asked him a single real question in three months. The next day she said, "Akash, I want you to build this mount. I'll check in every day." He nodded, and for the first time she saw him grin.

qa.q: What did Akash draw in the logbook margins?
qa.a: Neat redesigns of the sensor mount.

qa.q: What did Disha feel when she sat down heavily?
qa.a: She felt shocked and guilty, realising she had underestimated Akash and given him nothing to rise to.

qa.q: What does Disha's decision show about how to mentor juniors?
qa.a: Trusting someone with a real project and checking in daily gives them attention and a chance to grow.

qa.q: How might Akash see the new project?
qa.a: Akash seems pleased and encouraged, grinning for the first time as he is finally trusted.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing how giving challenging work to one junior and simple tasks to another shaped their growth.

passage: Career centre note, Tuesday. Chaitanya came back after the bank interview, looking flat. He'd told me last week, "I'll mess it up, I always do." He didn't come to the two mock sessions I offered. His friend Keerthana, who sat in the waiting room with him, said he had been scrolling his phone the night before instead of reading the job description. In the interview he said he couldn't answer the first question and then barely looked up. "See? I knew it," he told me. I pointed out, gently, that the fear had kept him from preparing and had shown in the room. He didn't argue. What I did next: booked two mock interviews for next week and asked Keerthana to come as the practice panel.

qa.q: How many mock sessions did Chaitanya skip?
qa.a: The two mock sessions.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling before and after the interview?
qa.a: He was afraid and anxious beforehand, sure he would fail, and afterwards flat and defeated, taking it as proof.

qa.q: How did the note-writer try to break the pattern?
qa.a: By gently naming how the fear led to little preparation, then booking two mock interviews with Keerthana as the practice panel.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Chaitanya's night before the interview?
qa.a: Keerthana probably felt worried watching him scroll instead of preparing, as if he had already given up.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult convinced the interview would go badly, preparing little and then seeing the failure as confirmation.

passage:
Thursday
The interview was at eleven. I knew by Monday it would go badly; I'm terrible at interviews. Thomas offered to do a practice round with me and I said no, what's the point. Last night I read the company page for ten minutes and gave up. This morning my hands shook so much I spilled tea on my file. In the room, they asked why I wanted the job and I said, "I'm not sure." I actually said that. They thanked me in five minutes flat. So, exactly as predicted. I told Thomas and he said, "You didn't prepare, Kalyani. That's not the same as being terrible." I was angry. I'm still angry. But he might have a point.

qa.q: What did Kalyani spill tea on?
qa.a: The file.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel on the morning of the interview?
qa.a: Kalyani felt very anxious, hands shaking, and already convinced of failing.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do before the next interview?
qa.a: Kalyani could accept Thomas's practice round and prepare properly, to test whether the prediction really holds.

qa.q: How does Thomas see what happened?
qa.a: Thomas sees it as a lack of preparation driven by fear, not proof that Kalyani is terrible at interviews.

grounding: Shows a young adult certain an interview will fail, preparing little, doing poorly, and taking it as confirmation.

passage: Before the team's quarterly dinner at the office canteen, Arohi caught the old thought: nobody will talk to me, I'll sit in a corner. She'd believed it for a year, and it had usually come true. This time she tried an experiment. She arrived early and spoke first to the new intern, asking about his project. Then she joined Arnab's table and asked about the client launch. People answered. Someone laughed at her joke. At the end, Arnab said, "You should come to the planning meeting." On the bus home, Arohi wrote in her phone notes: forecast, ignored; result, three real conversations. The next morning, when the intern's report was weak, she told him plainly what to fix, because she believed he could.

qa.q: Who did Arohi speak to first at the dinner?
qa.a: The new intern.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling as she walked into the canteen?
qa.a: She felt nervous and doubtful, expecting to be ignored, but determined to test the old belief.

qa.q: Why was writing down the forecast and the result useful?
qa.a: It let Arohi treat the evening as new evidence against the old belief rather than relying on the fear.

qa.q: How might the intern feel when Arohi told him plainly what to fix?
qa.a: He may feel challenged but respected, sensing she believes he can do better.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a gloomy forecast, acting against it by speaking first, treating the results as evidence, and holding others to fair expectations.

passage:
Dear Simran,
Remember how I said I'd bomb the budget presentation? I caught myself doing the usual thing: not preparing because "it'll go badly anyway." So this time I tried the opposite. I practised three times in front of the mirror and once in front of my roommate, who asked the nastiest questions she could think of. I wrote down my fear, "I'll freeze and they'll think I'm useless", and kept it in my pocket. I didn't freeze. I stumbled once and kept going. My manager asked one hard question and I actually had the answer. I'm not saying I'm cured. But I've got one piece of evidence against my old prediction now. That feels big.
Gargi

qa.q: How many times did Gargi practise in front of the mirror?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel after the presentation?
qa.a: Gargi feels relieved and quietly proud, holding one real piece of evidence against the old fear.

qa.q: What steps helped Gargi break the loop?
qa.a: Noticing the habit of not preparing, practising several times, writing down the fear, and then treating the result as new evidence.

qa.q: How might Simran react to the letter?
qa.a: Simran would likely feel happy and proud of Gargi, remembering the earlier prediction of bombing.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who notices a gloomy forecast, prepares well against it, and treats the result as new evidence.

passage: Sharmila, you asked how I survived your cousin's wedding when I knew nobody. Honestly, I went in with the old script: they'll think I'm dull, I'll stand by the wall. Every time I've believed that, I've stood by the wall, and then felt proved right. So this time I made one rule. Speak first, three times. I went up to your uncle and asked about the band. I asked your aunt how she'd made the sweets. I told a kid his dance moves were great. Three conversations. By dessert your uncle was introducing me as "the one who likes music." It wasn't magic. I was still nervous. But the evidence was different from the script. So I, Eshaan, am updating the script.

qa.q: What did Eshaan ask Sharmila's uncle about?
qa.a: The band.

qa.q: How was Eshaan feeling while going to the wedding?
qa.a: Eshaan felt nervous, expecting to be seen as dull, but chose to act against that fear.

qa.q: What was the "speak first, three times" rule, and why did it work?
qa.a: It meant starting three conversations instead of waiting by the wall, which gave people a chance to respond and produced new evidence.

qa.q: How does Sharmila's uncle seem to see Eshaan by dessert?
qa.a: He sees Eshaan as friendly and interesting, introducing Eshaan as "the one who likes music."

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing an expectation of being ignored, speaking first in small ways, and treating results as new evidence.

passage: Class 4 note, monsoon week. The spelling test came back today, and both Tushar and Sunaina failed it. Rain was hammering on the windows. Tushar put his head down and said, "I'm stupid. I'm always stupid at spellings." He didn't open his book again. Sunaina frowned at her paper and said, "I didn't learn the second page. I thought it wasn't in the test." She started copying the words she'd missed. What I did next: I sat with Tushar and showed him that he got every word right from the first page. "So what happened with the second page?" He thought. "I didn't practise those." "That's something you can fix." He picked his pencil up again, slowly.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say she didn't learn?
qa.a: The second page.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he put his head down?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and ashamed, believing he is always stupid at spellings.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do to help Tushar try again?
qa.a: Showed him he got the first page right and helped him see that not practising the second page was fixable.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's reaction differ from Tushar's?
qa.a: Sunaina saw the failure as a temporary cause, so she felt it could be fixed and started practising straight away.

grounding: Illustrates two children explaining the same failure as permanent or temporary, and how that shapes whether they try again.

passage:
Wednesday, in Ramzan
Today I got four out of fifteen in the maths test. I wanted to cry. I thought, I'm just stupid at maths. I'll never get it. At iftar I didn't even want dates. But Elizabeth failed too, and at break she just said, "Well, I didn't study fractions. I'll do that chapter this weekend." She wasn't even sad. And I thought, wait. I didn't study fractions either. We were at Nani's all Saturday. Maybe it's not that I'm stupid. Maybe it's just fractions I haven't done yet. Tomorrow I'll ask Abbu to help me with them after iftar. I feel a bit better now.
Noor

qa.q: What score did Noor get in the maths test?
qa.a: Four out of fifteen.

qa.q: How did Noor's feelings change after talking to Elizabeth?
qa.a: Noor went from feeling hopeless and stupid to feeling a bit better, seeing the failure as fixable.

qa.q: What is Noor's plan, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Asking Abbu for help with fractions after iftar, because it targets the actual cause of the low mark.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's way of explaining the failure help her?
qa.a: Seeing it as an unstudied chapter lets Elizabeth stay calm and try again that weekend.

grounding: Shows a child moving from "I'm stupid" to "I didn't study that chapter" after seeing a friend's explanation.

passage: It was harvest season, and half the village school had been helping in the fields. When the test papers came back, Noor and Nilesh had both failed the sums. Nilesh crumpled his paper and threw it in the ditch on the way home. "My head's made of mud. Baba says so too." Noor, walking beside him with her sister, looked at her own red marks. "We missed the whole week of division. We were cutting paddy." "So?" "So we just don't know division yet. We're not mud." Her sister said, "Master stays after school on Thursdays." On Thursday, Noor stayed. Nilesh walked past the classroom window, slowed down, then kept going.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do with his paper?
qa.a: He crumpled it and threw it in the ditch on the way home.

qa.q: How was Nilesh feeling when he said his head was made of mud?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and ashamed, believing he was permanently bad at sums.

qa.q: What could help Nilesh try again, as Noor did?
qa.a: He could see the failure as missing a week of division, not a mud head, and stay back for Master's Thursday help.

qa.q: How does Noor's sister react to the failed sums?
qa.a: She stays practical and encouraging, telling them about Master's Thursday help after school.

grounding: Illustrates two children explaining the same failure as permanent or temporary, and who tries again as a result.

passage: Tomas didn't make the school band in Prague. Walking home, he laid out the case against himself. I'm bad at music. I'm bad at sports, too. I'm going to fail maths. Everything I try goes wrong, and it always will. He cancelled his guitar lesson that evening and put the case under the bed. Xin, who'd also auditioned and also missed out, messaged: "They only took two new people. I'll try again in spring. Want to practise together?" Tomas stared at the message. It seemed so simple for Xin. He typed, "What's the point," deleted it, typed it again. It felt like being realistic. It didn't occur to him that this was just one way of explaining one bad afternoon.

qa.q: How many new people did the band take?
qa.a: Only two new people.

qa.q: What was Tomas feeling as he walked home?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and defeated, blaming himself and believing that everything he tries will always go wrong.

qa.q: What could Tomas say to himself instead of "What's the point"?
qa.a: That only two places were open and it was one audition, and that practising with Xin before spring could change the result.

qa.q: How does Xin see the same audition?
qa.a: Xin sees it as temporary and specific, a limited number of places, and plans to try again in spring.

grounding: Shows a teenager who blames himself for a setback, sees it as permanent and everywhere, and gives up quickly.

passage: At the football academy hostel, Asif missed a penalty in the inter-hostel final. That night, he didn't come down for dinner. "I always choke," he told Suraj, his roommate, staring at the ceiling. "In football, in exams, everywhere. I'm just that kind of person." The next morning, he skipped practice. The morning after, too. "Why bother? Coach will never trust me again." Suraj said, "Coach said it was a good strike, the keeper just guessed right." Asif shook his head. "You're being nice." To Asif, this felt like honesty, seeing himself clearly at last. Suraj went down to breakfast alone and, worried, mentioned it to the coach, who came up to the room that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Asif miss in the inter-hostel final?
qa.a: A penalty.

qa.q: How was Asif feeling while staring at the ceiling?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and ashamed, convinced he always chokes and always will, everywhere.

qa.q: How could the coach help Asif see the miss differently?
qa.a: The coach could point to the good strike and the keeper's guess, and ask Asif back to practice to show one miss doesn't define him.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the missed penalty?
qa.a: Suraj sees it as bad luck, a good strike that the keeper guessed right, and is worried about his friend.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who explains a setback as permanent and all-pervasive and gives up quickly, believing it realism.

passage:
Charu,
You asked about the science test. I got 11 out of 40. That's it, I'm officially stupid. I've always been bad at science, and now it's spreading to everything. I'll probably fail maths next, then English, and then what? I stopped doing the revision sheets two days ago, what's the point. I know you'll say "it's just one test". But it doesn't feel like one test. It feels like finally seeing the truth. Mum says I'm being dramatic. Maybe. I just don't see how it changes. Remember last year when you told me I'm always hardest on myself? I keep thinking about that. I don't know if you're right.
Deepika

qa.q: What score did Deepika get in the science test?
qa.a: 11 out of 40.

qa.q: How is Deepika feeling about the test result?

passage: The results list went up on the college noticeboard in the kasba, and Parul's roll number wasn't in the accounts pass column. She walked home past the sugar mill with the old voice loud in her head: you're useless, you'll never pass. At home, her younger brother Nilesh asked, "Didi, what happened?" She told him. Then, instead of crying on the cot, she took out her paper and checked. The theory questions: good marks. The ledger problems: nearly zero. She remembered she had never finished the ledger chapter. "It's not all of accounts," she said aloud. "It's ledgers." Nilesh brought her tea. She wrote on the back of the paper: two ledger problems every day before the supplementary exam.

qa.a: The accounts pass column.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling on the walk home?

qa.a: He is concerned, asking what happened, and supportive, bringing her tea while she works it out.

passage: Ines got her organic chemistry grade in Lisbon on a rainy Friday: failed. For an hour she sat on the kitchen floor of the flat, thinking, I'm not smart enough for medicine, everyone knew it but me. Her roommate Daniel slid down next to her. "What's the story you're telling yourself?" "That I'm stupid." "And the evidence?" She thought. "I passed biology and physics this term. Well." "So what's different about chemistry?" "I studied alone. I never went to the problem sessions." "Anything else?" "I did the exam with a fever." She almost laughed. "So maybe not stupid." "Maybe not." She wrote one line on a sticky note: go to every problem session. She still felt bad. But now it was a fixable kind of bad.

qa.q: Which subjects did Ines pass this term?
qa.a: Biology and physics.

qa.q: How did Ines feel while sitting on the kitchen floor?
qa.a: She felt defeated and ashamed, telling herself she wasn't smart enough for medicine.

qa.q: What questions helped Ines check the story against the facts?
qa.a: Daniel asked what story she was telling herself, what the evidence was, and what was different about chemistry, which led her to one change.

qa.q: How does Daniel help without forcing her to cheer up?
qa.a: Daniel sits with her and asks questions rather than telling her it's fine, letting her find the evidence herself.

grounding: Shows a student who fails an exam questioning the evidence, considering other explanations and choosing one change.

passage: The school inspection was in two weeks, and the staff room felt it. Vaibhav, the youngest maths teacher, watched two colleagues get ready. Mr Kurian waved it off: "Everything will be fine. Inspectors never check registers properly." His registers had gaps from July. Sudha, the science teacher, said, "It could go well if we fix what's weak." She listed three problems on the whiteboard, took the lab safety one herself and asked who'd help with the others. "I think we can pull this off," she said. When the inspectors came, they asked for registers first. Mr Kurian's face fell. Sudha's lab passed without a note. Vaibhav noted how different their kinds of confidence had been, one a hope and one a plan.

qa.q: What did Sudha take on herself?
qa.a: The lab safety problem.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav be feeling as he watches the two colleagues?
qa.a: Vaibhav seems curious and thoughtful, and perhaps a little uneasy, noticing that Mr Kurian's cheerfulness ignores real risks.

qa.q: What made Sudha's approach work?
qa.a: She believed things could go well and backed that hope with a list of problems, a task for herself and a request for help.

qa.q: How might Mr Kurian feel when the inspectors ask for registers?

passage:
Dear Swati,
You asked about the new job. The strangest thing is watching two people on my team react to the same news. Our biggest client might leave next quarter. My manager keeps saying, "It'll be fine, they love us," and changes the subject. No plan, nothing. Then there's Kavin, who's my age. He said, "I think we can keep them, but not by hoping." He called the client, asked what was bothering them, and made a list of fixes. He's cheerful too, but his cheer comes with a spreadsheet. I trust his version more. I've started helping him with the list. I'll tell you how it turns out.
Neelam

qa.q: What might happen with the biggest client next quarter?
qa.a: The client might leave.

qa.q: How does Neelam feel about the two reactions?
qa.a: Neelam feels uneasy with the manager's "It'll be fine" and more trusting and hopeful about Kavin's approach.

qa.q: Why is Kavin's approach wiser than the manager's?
qa.a: He combines hope with action, calling the client to find out what's wrong and listing fixes.

qa.q: How might Swati read this letter?
qa.a: Swati might see that Neelam is learning to tell empty reassurance from real, prepared hope.

grounding: Shows a young adult observing blind reassurance next to hope backed by planning.

passage: Shalini, you know my two cousins who run the shops in the market? Let me tell you what I saw this monsoon. The weather warnings came out: heavy rain, possible flooding in the low lanes. Arvind Bhaiya laughed. "Nothing will happen. Never has." He left his rice sacks on the floor. Chhaya Didi said, "I think we'll be okay, but let's be ready." She lifted her stock onto crates and wrapped the fridge motor in plastic. The water came up to the knee. Arvind Bhaiya lost half his rice. Chhaya Didi opened her shutter the next morning and sold tea to the whole lane. I, Indu, learned something: hope is good. Hope with crates is better.

qa.q: How high did the water come?
qa.a: Up to the knee.

qa.q: How does Indu seem to feel about what happened to the two cousins?
qa.a: Indu seems thoughtful and a little sad for Arvind Bhaiya, and impressed by how Chhaya Didi's hope came with preparation.

qa.q: What did Chhaya Didi do that made the difference?
qa.a: She lifted her stock onto crates and wrapped the fridge motor, preparing for the risk while still hoping for the best.

qa.q: How might Arvind Bhaiya feel the morning after?
qa.a: He probably feels shocked and regretful, having lost half his rice by assuming nothing would happen.

grounding: Illustrates an observer comparing a cousin's naive reassurance with another's hopeful preparation.

passage:
Dear Kamal,
I read your message three times. You said you're a failure, that three years of preparing for the civil services have been wasted, and that you should just give up. I'm not going to tell you to cheer up. It sounds really painful, and I'm here. But can I help you sort it a bit? Some things are fixed: this attempt is over, the results are out. Some things aren't: your notes, your knowledge, the attempts you have left, what you want next. You don't have to decide your whole future this week. What's one small thing you could do by Sunday? Maybe just meet me for chai. I'm coming over on Saturday either way.
Saurabh

qa.q: How many years has Kamal been preparing for the civil services?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: How does Saurabh seem to feel reading Kamal's message?
qa.a: Saurabh feels concerned and caring, taking Kamal's pain seriously rather than brushing it off.

qa.q: How does Saurabh help Kamal without dismissing the despair?
qa.a: Saurabh acknowledges the pain, separates what is fixed from what can change, and suggests one small step by Sunday.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Kamal might feel less alone and a little lighter, with something small to do instead of a whole future to decide.

grounding: Shows a young adult listening to a friend's despair, separating fixed from changeable, and suggesting one small step.

passage: So when Nandini's little bakery shut down, she called me at midnight. I'm Deepak, her friend since college, and I'm usually the guy who says "it'll be fine." This time I didn't. I just listened. She said she'd wasted her savings, disappointed her parents, that she's not a business person. I said, "That sounds awful." And I meant it. Then, the next day, over tea, I asked, "What can't you change?" The shop's closed. The loan's there. "What can you?" She thought. "My recipes are still good. People still ask for my cakes." "So what's one small thing?" She said she could take two orders from home this month. Not a new shop. Just two orders. She did five.

qa.q: How many orders did Nandini end up doing?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: How was Nandini feeling when she called at midnight?
qa.a: She felt despairing and ashamed, sure she had wasted her savings and disappointed her parents.

qa.q: What did Deepak do differently from his usual "it'll be fine"?
qa.a: He listened first and agreed it sounded awful, then helped Nandini separate what was fixed from what could change and pick one small step.

qa.q: What would change if Deepak had said "it'll be fine" as usual?
qa.a: Nandini might have felt dismissed and alone with her despair, and might never have found the small step of taking orders from home.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult listening to a friend's despair without dismissing it and helping her find one small next step.

passage: I'm Tenzin, Kishore's flatmate, and I was in the kitchen the night Hafsa came over after her design firm rejected her. She was crying and saying she'd never be good enough. Kishore didn't jump in with advice. He made tea and just said, "That really hurts." He let her talk for a long time. Then he pulled a notebook over. "Okay. Let's split it. What's done?" "The rejection." "What's still yours?" "My portfolio. My contacts." "One thing for this week?" She said she'd ask them for feedback. I don't know what she felt when she left, but she was sitting up straighter. Kishore told me later he'd been scared she'd think he wasn't listening. She didn't.

qa.q: What did Kishore make before talking to Hafsa?
qa.a: Tea.

qa.q: What does Kishore's later comment reveal about his feelings?
qa.a: He had been scared and anxious that Hafsa might feel unheard if he moved too quickly to planning.

qa.q: How did Kishore help without dismissing Hafsa's despair?
qa.a: He listened first, then helped her split what was done from what was still hers and choose one step: asking for feedback.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see the evening afterwards?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel supported and steadier, having found her own next step while being heard.

grounding: Shows an observer describing a young adult who listens to a discouraged friend and helps separate what is fixed from what can change.

passage: "Merry Christmas, everyone!" The cousins crowded the living room. A balloon popped. Joseph's lip wobbled, and he wailed. Across the rug, little Wasim stopped stacking cups and stared at Joseph. His face crumpled too. "Why is Wasim crying?" Aunty asked. "He didn't even hear the pop." "He heard Joseph," said Mama, scooping up both boys. "Shh, shh." Joseph sniffled into her shoulder. Wasim watched him, then sniffled too.

qa.q: What popped?
qa.a: A balloon popped.

qa.q: Why did Wasim's face crumple?
qa.a: He seemed upset and worried just from seeing and hearing Joseph cry, even though he didn't know about the pop.

qa.q: What did Mama do that helped?
qa.a: She scooped up both boys together and soothed them, calming the shared distress.

qa.q: How might Aunty see Wasim's crying?
qa.a: Aunty is puzzled, since Wasim didn't hear the pop, not realising crying spreads between little ones.

grounding: Illustrates one toddler's crying spreading to another who does not know the cause.

passage: Nursery note, Monday. At drop-off, Mohit clung to the gate and cried hard. Within a minute, two toddlers near the blocks stopped playing. One began to whimper; the other looked around with a worried face. Neither knew why. Mohit's big sister Reena, who had brought him, looked unsure. "Did I upset them?" I told her no. We sat Mohit on the mat with a picture book and sang softly. The whimpering faded as Mohit calmed. Reena smiled, relieved.

qa.q: Where did Mohit cling while crying?
qa.a: To the gate.

qa.q: What did the two toddlers near the blocks seem to feel?
qa.a: They seemed worried and upset, catching Mohit's distress without knowing why.

qa.q: What helped all the children settle?
qa.a: Calming Mohit with a picture book and soft singing, which eased the others as well.

qa.q: How did Reena feel watching the other toddlers react?
qa.a: She felt unsure and a little guilty at first, then relieved when they calmed.

grounding: Shows a toddler's crying spreading to others at nursery who do not know why.

passage: At the village anganwadi, the ceiling fan stopped with a clank. Hafsa jumped and began to cry. Her cousin Kishore, sitting beside her on the mat, looked at her face, then puckered up and cried too. Soon a third child was whimpering. Their older cousin, waiting by the door, laughed softly. "Kishore, you weren't even scared!" The helper picked up Hafsa and swayed. As she quieted, Kishore quieted too.

qa.q: What made the clank?
qa.a: The ceiling fan stopped with a clank.

qa.q: What does Kishore puckering up suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt upset and worried just from seeing Hafsa cry, not from the noise.

qa.q: What did the helper do that calmed both children?
qa.a: She picked up Hafsa and swayed, and as Hafsa quieted, Kishore did too.

qa.q: How does the older cousin react to the crying?
qa.a: The older cousin finds it gently funny, noticing that Kishore wasn't even scared.

grounding: Illustrates how one toddler's crying makes another toddler cry without knowing why.
